utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Since Judge Nieto-Navia has no ear phones, we'll have to wait for a second. Good morning to everyone on what will be the last day of this trial. Today, the bench will put questions to the parties and ask for clarifications on issues that are not yet clear to us. I'd like to start with one question and ask both parties about it. Perhaps first the Prosecution. My question is about the agreement of the 22nd of May of 1992. I take it that you're aware of the agreement I refer to at this moment. May I ask the Prosecution first whether the Prosecution takes the view that this agreement entered into force because all ratifications were there?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Mr. Mundis will respond to any questions that you have in relation to the law so I'll hand over to Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, what's the view on the completeness of the ratifications in view of Article 6, paragraph 2 of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution does in fact take the view that the agreement which the parties have signed entered into force pursuant to the terms of Article 6 of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence what their position is?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has some doubt. We remember a witness who pointed out this issue that we didn't raise but there was a witness that indicated that certain agreements had in fact been obtained and actually signed by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic but that they weren't ratified in a technical sense of the term, and as a result, had not entered into force. So it is an open question and it is not for the Defence to respond to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, in your pre-trial brief you said that the agreement was valid and you did not give any reasons in respect of ratifications why it would not be valid in your final brief so a clarification on your part would not -- would not something -- would not be something that would be beyond what could have been asked from the Defence. Mr. Mundis, was this agreement ratified by Croatia, as far as you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not aware of Croatia having ratified this agreement but as the Prosecution in our written submissions has made clear, which, if you'd like to be -- like me to be heard on, I can elaborate upon, the Prosecution also would have the position that this agreement, even if the special agreement is not in force, that the parties are nevertheless bond pursuant to Additional Protocol I itself and that those provisions do reflect customary international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's a -- the question is now whether this agreement would apply or not because you refer to Article 6 of the agreement and said that the terms of Article 6, the agreement would be -- would have entered into force, whereas Article 6 reads that the agreement will enter into force on the 26th of May, if all parties have transmitted to the ICRC their formal acceptance of the agreement by the 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the reference on the first page of this document to the Croatian Democratic Community of course is the HDZ within Bosnia-Herzegovina. This agreement between the parties represents the three factions within Bosnia-Herzegovina so the Prosecution would contend that Croatia was not a party to this agreement and thus the issue of whether or not Croatia agreed to the terms of the agreement is not really at issue in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do I then understand you well that the ratification by the -- by Bosnia-Herzegovina would cover also the Croatian party to this agreement or the Croatian --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, the penultimate point we agree on the penultimate point with the Prosecution. And we don't see why this document should have been ratified, either by Croatia or any other state, with the exception of BH, that is to say Bosnia and Herzegovina, since the three other parties were not states, they were political parties, political organisations, but certainly not states, so I think that we have managed to reach a substantial agreement on this issue. The Prosecution and the Defence have reached an agreement, no ratification could have been in effect because we are not talking about states and I'm referring to the signatories after the first.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to add something. I just wanted to add something to what my learned colleague has just said with regard to clarification -- clarifying Protocol I, that is to say the signed agreement, its implementation, apart from the fact that my colleague pointed out that the agreement was ratified by party representatives not by states, not by state representatives but by party representatives I would like to say that Bosnia and Herzegovina is not a successor state of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and that Yugoslavia doesn't have anything to do with the signed agreement. And that that agreement which was signed by the representatives of these political parties doesn't provide for the implementation of Protocol I but only for some of the principles that relate to civilians in Protocol I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would this influence in whatever way the binding effect of this agreement to the conflict? The parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've set forth in our written submissions the position that Bosnia-Herzegovina was in fact a state party to Additional Protocol I and pursuant to both the four, 1949 Geneva Conventions and the Additional Protocols which set forth provisions that permit parties to sign special agreements, that this special agreement in fact was supplemental to the four, 1949 Geneva Conventions and the two Additional Protocols there to and that on the basis of Bosnia-Herzegovina being a state party to those agreements, and this special agreement of 22 May, 1992, that in fact, the three, if you will, warring parties within Bosnia-Herzegovina pursuant to the terms of this special agreement thereby made the terms of Additional Protocol I which are specified this in agreement applicable to the armed conflict on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then -- you're referring to Bosnia and Herzegovina as a party to the four Geneva Conventions and Protocol II and Protocol II. For Protocol I of course that would suggest that the conflict was of an international character.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Of course Additional Protocol I by its terms only applies to an international armed conflict. However the Prosecution position is that this agreement made those specific provisions applicable in a non-international armed conflict as evidenced by the fact that it was three internal political parties within Bosnia-Herzegovina who specifically agreed to abide by those provisions notwithstanding the fact that the treaty, Additional Protocol I would otherwise not be applicable by its terms to the conflict in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was the last part of your answer that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, since you have in your last answer -- Mr. Mundis, sorry that I'm making a mistake. Everyone has his own problems. I'm mixing you up. You were emphasising that it was through this 22nd of May agreement that Additional Protocol I would be applicable but nevertheless, Article 6 says that all parties should have transmitted their formal acceptance of the agreement by the 22nd -- the 26th of May, 1992 and that brings us back to the first question: What about the formal acceptance, I called it the ratification, but I should have spoken about formal acceptance rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no evidence of the transmittal of formal acceptance to the ICRC. We do of course have evidence based on this document that the parties agreed to these terms but we simply do not at this point have evidence before this Trial Chamber that in fact this purely technical issue of transmitting the agreement to the ICRC by the 26th of May actually happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If, just for argument's sake, we would assume that the Croatian Democratic Community would not have transmitted their formal acceptance to the ICRC, would that affect the binding force of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, pursuant to the terms of Article 6 of this agreement, it clearly states all parties so that would by the terms of the agreement result in the fact that the agreement would not have been entered into force. Again, at this point the Prosecution would rely on the fact that the parties have signed the agreement, as evidenced by Prosecution Exhibit 58, clearly demonstrating an intent to be bound by the terms set forth in the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I have the view of the Defence on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It seems and we mentioned this a minute ago, but the Defence is not in a position to answer this question and what you spoke -- what you mentioned as a ratification, I don't think I could intervene on that point. I see that the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I noticed that the Prosecution doesn't know very well whether these -- the four necessary ratifications were implemented or not and if the formal acceptance of this was necessary and was not implemented then obviously the legal consequences should be noted. Otherwise the act might not be complete, if it didn't have all the necessary -- if all the necessary preconditions hadn't been met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if let's just assume that the parties to the -- who had transmitted their formal acceptance to this agreement, if these parties would have acted in accordance with this agreement, for example, I draw your attention to article 5, implementation, each party undertakes to designate liaison officers to the ICRC. If for example, the parties who had transmitted their formal acceptance would have appointed such liaison officers, would that change anything in the view of the Defence, although your answer was not very clear, you said the legal consequences had to be drawn from the fact that it was not -- you didn't say what the legal consequences were but if you would assume that liaison officers were appointed, would that change anything in the legal consequences to be drawn?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, that would change the whole history of these proceedings, not just in legal terms but in factual terms because there would have been a mechanism of immediate information, and we wouldn't be here in such a case. I will just confer for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In legal terms, of course, that wouldn't have much of an effect we would certainly agree on that. But what I wanted to say is that if these mechanisms of information had actually been functioning as they should have functioned, we certainly wouldn't be here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could briefly make two points. First, it's a generally recognised principle of international law that states and I would argue by analogy this agreement would fall within that category, that states which have signed agreements pending formal ratification are bound to an adhere to the terms of their agreement and to do nothing which would be contrary to the express agreements which they have reached while the ratification and notification process is pending. First we would say that this treaty or this special agreement would be analogous to a treaty in that respect with respect to that general principle of international law. Second, the issue particularly with respect to whether or not the HDZ ratified this agreement or in fact all three of the parties transmitted their acceptance of this agreement to the ICRC, is an issue which is not in the Prosecution's submission arisen during the course of this trial. It was not an issue which the Defence specifically addressed in great detail in their written submissions and the Prosecution, if it would be of assistance to the Chamber, would seek leave to attempt to put additional evidence before the Chamber with respect to the agreement and transmittal of the parties' agreement to the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that. May I first ask you, Mr. Mundis, whether it results from the first part of your answer that on from the 26th of May, since the parties were supposed to transmit their formal acceptance by the 26th of May, that after the 26th, the agreement could be considered not -- at least that the parties could not be expected to act in accordance with the -- with the agreement, because you said that during the ratification period, which ends on the 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with all due respect the Prosecution would submit that the 26 May, 1992, 1800 hours deadline was simply an administrative detail, if you will, and that in fact the date of this agreement, 22 May, 1992, would be the date upon which the obligations of the parties would begin to run and that in fact that date would or that agreement would remain in force from that date afterwards, and that the transmittal to the ICRC of their formal acceptance was purely an administrative detail so that the agreement could be placed on file with the ICRC, which as the Chamber is aware, is the designated depository institution for the four, 1949 Geneva Conventions and the two Additional Protocols there to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Referring to the second part of your answer, you said the issue was not raised during trial. Is it the position of the Prosecution that as far as the applicable law is concerned, that the Chamber should follow the parties if they would agree on the applicable law where the Chamber might have doubts as to the applicable law or might have a different position? I mean is it something that is in the realm of the parties to agree upon or is it something the Chamber should --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Certainly the applicability of the law, Mr. President, is an issue for the Trial Chamber but it would seem that if in the event the parties have agreed on what the applicable law is that that would certainly inform the Trial Chamber's decision, but clearly, the applicability of the law or the law which this Chamber will apply is a question for this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask the Defence whether they share this view? The last part. Whether you share the view that where the parties are not contradicting each other, I'm not saying that they are not, but if they would agree on the applicable law, that nevertheless it would be for the Chamber to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not sure that the parties always agree on the applicable law. What I said a minute ago was that it wasn't for the Defence to respond to this issue. We have provided certain elements so we have certain opinions, but we saw that we don't agree on applicable law. For example, when we arrive on conclusions as -- with regard to Protocol 1 or Protocol 2, et cetera, et cetera. In such cases with regard to such issues we can see that the parties are not in agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber noticed that you did agree but that you do not agree any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this moment on this issue but the other judges might have additional questions and might have other questions as well so I'd first like to ask Judge Nieto-Navia to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I will start the question to Mr. Mundis regarding the -- what he said on the analogy of this agreement with the law of treaties. You said, Mr. Mundis, that before the ratification of a treaty, the parties are bound to the terms of the agreement and shouldn't do anything which is contrary to the agreement. I agree with you on the second part, according to the law of treaties to the Vienna convention but if the first part, that is that the parties were bound or are bound to the agreement, which is the purpose of the ratification?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would seem that the -- that in many national jurisdictions, ratification is required so that the -- particularly with respect to non-self-executing treaties, it would seem that the primary purpose of the ratification process is to ensure that the -- in those systems which require ratification for the treaty to be accepted as a legal institution within the state, within its domestic system that that's the primary purpose of the ratification of the treaty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: So the primary purpose is not to give a definite concept -- the definite approval to the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It would give the definite agreement of the state to the terms of the treaty by ensuring that the full weight of the state's legal institutions are behind the state's agreement to be bound by the terms of the treaty so that it's an important -- ratification serves to ensure that a state is fully bound or expresses its intent to be fully bound by the agreement with the full weight of the national legal institutions in support of what typically the executive has done in signing the treaty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: You said that you considered the ratification is just an administrative detail. Okay. I have some questions on the other issues, unless Judge El Mahdi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If I may have your leave, I don't think it is true to say that the ratification is simply the execution. I think my learned colleague confuses what we call the instrumentation of the ratification of the law, the ratification itself is superior to the one that when it's just concluded. So that the act in question can be redressed in all the necessary forms according to its existence, and that to a superior level, in general, to the ones that -- to those that establish the actual act. And I'm sorry for interrupting. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, I'd like to draw your attention to the formulation used of the Article 6, paragraph 2 of the agreement of the 22nd of May, 1992. If we look at this carefully, we can see that the parties do reserve the right of applying the agreement if all the parties, and I will now quote in English, [In English] "The present agreement will enter into force on 26 May at 24 hours if all parties have transmitted." [Interpretation] Which could indicate that it wasn't simply a formality, as you say, a formality, to ratify this agreement but the parties expressly reserved the right to not apply this agreement, not implement it, unless all of the parties to the agreement transmit their ratification. Does that change your opinion somewhat, if you can give me your position in the light of this formulation in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could, I think that the continuation of that paragraph is important to understand the Prosecution position. Article 6, paragraph 2, continues that the parties have transmitted to the ICRC their formal acceptance of the agreement, and it is that formal acceptance which represents the national authorities or in this case the parties, the political parties' putting their full weight behind what the senior representatives of those parties have agreed to, and in fact, the specific language of this provision indicates that what is required by the 26th of May at 1992 at 1800 is their formal acceptance and the Prosecution would argue that the parties have accepted this agreement on the 22nd of May and what then remains to be done is simply a formal acceptance to be given by the 26th of May. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So you don't make a distinction, you don't differentiate between the signatures put on the agreement on the formal acceptance? Rather the signing of the agreement on the formal acceptance? It's a draft agreement? Or is it an agreement which is executive in itself and which doesn't have to have other formalities? I have some difficulties following this, following the language of this paragraph, which says basically what it boils down to, that the agreement itself is applicable regardless of the conditions because it seems to me that the language expresses that [In English] their formal acceptance [Interpretation] it does indicate or it could indicate that the agreement is just -- this agreement is just a provisional agreement, it is not a formal agreement, so with all the possible consequences, legal consequences, it isn't or it might not be possible to be executed, to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the point as to whether it's a draft agreement, the Prosecution would be of the position that it's certainly not a draft agreement, it's been signed and no where on the face of the agreement do we see any indication that it is a draft agreement. Rather, the signatures on the bottom of the agreement would indicate that it is not a draft agreement. With respect to whether or not it's an executing or non-self-executing document, the Prosecution's position is that the document simply required transmittal to the ICRC of the formal acceptance by a certain date, as indicated by the document, and that that formal acceptance was merely an administrative detail which would permit the ICRC to be in possession of the formal acceptance as the depository institution for agreements, special agreements, as well as the four Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocols there to. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very last observation, please, I'm sorry, but what you are saying is that you're interpreting the express language that the present agreement will enter into force if all parties [In English] have transmitted to the ICRC their formal acceptance [Interpretation] as not having legal consequences, that the agreement is applicable whether the parties have transmitted their acceptance of the agreement or not. Is that what your position is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, prior to answering that, if I could have a very brief moment to consult, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if this issue would raise further issues that would need consultation, we might have a break then later on, and then you might come up with responses after that short break. Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as the Defence is concerned, I think there is no need to confer because I think we can see the thing simply, matters simply. This is not a question of it being a draft. It's just the implementation or not. What we call a technically suspensive condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to give an opportunity to Judge Nieto-Navia to put any other questions or perhaps that are related to this issue but it's not the only issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think that these questions should be answered by Mr. Ierace but I will not break my lance for that. The first question is the following. Speaking on the 6th of May about incident 22, Mr. Ierace said that the Prosecutor could not assert the place where the bullet came from, and you added, but it is not important. If you don't know where the bullet came from, how can you charge that crime to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. When I said that, I should have made more clearly -- made clear the position of the Prosecution, which is that it does not matter where specifically on the territory held by the SRK the bullet came from. In other words, one must be mindful of specifically what it is that the Prosecution sets out to prove in relation to the scheduled sniping incidents. Your Honour, the Prosecution does not set out to establish the identity of the particular subordinate of the accused who fired the bullet. The Prosecution invites the Trial Chamber to take into consideration other relevant bodies of evidence, such as that, in relation to this specific scheduled incident, the Sarajevo Romania Corps held the territory of the Nedzarici, that within that territory, the accused enjoyed command and control of his subordinates, right down to the level of those responsible for operating the infantry weapons. It certainly matters whether the bullet came from the side of the confrontation lines controlled by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps but once it's established it came from that side, thereafter it's of no consequence whether the bullet came from the school of theology or from somewhere on the territory between the school of theology and the confrontation lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. We are now speaking about incident number 13. You said that even if the father was a combatant, the victim was a 15-years-old child. My question is: Given the circumstances of the case, that there was a barrier, that the truck was going at some speed, you said 20 to 30 kilometres, could a sniper be aware of the fact that there was a 15-year-old child in the truck?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, I think that it's important to consider on the basis of the evidence, what picture presented itself to the person responsible for firing the bullet. We can deduce from the evidence that the sniper would have observed a truck with no military markings, indeed specifically some civilian markings, that is that it was a butcher's truck, butcher being written on the side of the truck. No military equipment around, except for the French APC vehicle that was 100 metres further up the road. The occupants of the vehicle, only two, weren't dressed in military uniform, no weapons were there. So if one places oneself in the position of the shooter, the first question to be asked is: What was it about that potential target that indicated it was a legitimate target, that one or both of the occupants were combatants? And the answer to that is nothing. One must then allow for the possibility, as remote as it seems on the evidence, that the shooter had some personal information that led him to believe that one or both of the occupants were in fact combatants. There is no evidence at all to suggest that but let's assume for the sake of the argument that there was some knowledge that the shooter had that the driver was a combatant. The next step in our process of thinking is, well, how does the principle of proportionality apply to that situation, if he had that personal knowledge? The situation that then presents itself is that the passenger was not a combatant, certainly was not a combatant. He may or may not have discerned his age, the fact that he was a child, from that distance and so on, but one must apply the, for lack of a better term, the standard of proof that's required as a result of Article 13. In other words, the shooter must have removed any doubt that the target is a military target and then consider whether the principle of proportionality would be offended. I don't suggest for a minute that a shooter would think of it in these formal, technical terms but rather put more simply, would it be appropriate to target a combatant when in the same line of sight or very close to it is someone who is not known to be a combatant? A very high risk is involved, which is demonstrated by the fact that the bullet hit the door of the truck. So the Prosecution says that firstly there were no military indicia and if there was any personal knowledge, unfounded as it in fact was, that the driver was not a proper target in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: My question arose because you stressed the fact that the victim was a 15-years-old child. That was the origin of the question. Of course I understand that the truck was not marked with -- so, okay. Thank you. Speaking about the orders received by the SRK troops once a week, not to target civilians, you said the following: That is inconsistent, if they were not targeting civilians, why the orders? Those are your words. Would you have a better or a worse case if they wouldn't have received those orders?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The Prosecution does not accept the evidence that they received those orders. The Prosecution does that because it has regard to the evidence of Witness D and another witness who will remain unnamed, evidence which is inconsistent with that aspect of these Defence witnesses so the Prosecution first seeks to point out the inconsistency within that aspect of the Defence evidence. Why would they receive those orders with such frequency if they weren't targeting civilians? Whether we would have a better or worse case, if it wasn't for that evidence, I suppose it could be said that there would be -- it would be a better case for the Prosecution if that evidence didn't exist at all but given the evidence, one must first decide what weight to attribute to it. The Prosecution says no weight for the reason I've indicated, and Prosecution submits therefore that having done that analysis, the Prosecution is no worse off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: On incident 25, you said, and I think that we have evidence on that, that the victim was warned by ABiH soldiers because there was some shooting in the area. My question is: If there was a combat, could you speak of the liberated targeting of civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's I think important to recall the precise evidence in that regard, which was this: The witness said that she and her girlfriend approached the road, some ABiH soldiers on a balcony called out to them that snipers were active, snipers were active. She gave no evidence of any fire emanating from the ABiH side. So when one talks about -- first I think one has to assess what was the action that was occurring before she entered that scene together with the victim. The evidence in that regard I would respectfully submit does not allow one to conclude that there was lawful armed combat in place at all. It may be that the snipers were targeting combatants before she and her friend sought to cross the street. It may not be. It's open in that sense. But the question then comes back to again the principles of distinction and proportionality. If we place ourselves in the position of the shooter, let's assume that he had previously, he or she, been engaged in lawful targeting of ABiH combatants in that area. It was manifestly obvious, the Prosecution submits, that there were civilians living in the same area. He had an obligation, a duty to target with that in mind, to remove any doubt that these targets were combatants, and here we have not only the age of the two girls at the time but also their appearance, both had evidence as to the length of their hair, their clothes and so on, no military clothing involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that the shooting that you spoke about was sniper's fire, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Those were the words. The evidence was they were the words used, "there was snipers active".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Speaking of the about the Kosevo hospital you said there that no military were hit, only civilians, and your conclusion was was that it was retaliatory, not counterbattery fire. My question is whether retaliatory fire is allowed in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, is the short answer to that, Your Honour. We heard evidence as to what is meant by the term counterbattery fire. That is a behaviour which makes perfect sense from a military perspective. To retaliate in the sense of hitting an unlawful target, is certainly -- well, as I've indicated by the terms, that's an unlawful form of behaviour, and one has to analyse the evidence in relation to the nature of the return fire, the timing, what it actually hit, whether it succeeded in neutralising the mortars over a very long period of time, almost two years, in order to deduce, we submit, quite confidently that it was retaliatory and not counterbattery. If I could say this also in relation to your question, Your Honour, having regard to the precise wording of your question, whether retaliatory fire is allowed in war, these are terms, retaliatory fire, counterbattery fire, I think it's important to have regard to the specific circumstances beyond that terminology as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Well, I have a short question and I am looking for a short answer: Who did control the sport stadium?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Which one? There were two. There was the stadium near Hrasno and there was a stadium to the north near the Kosevo hospital. I take it you mean Hrasno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In -- well, I can keep my answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: We heard evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. And the evidence that it was the ABiH included not only General Karavelic but civilians and soldiers who lived in Hrasno, such as Mrs. Mukanovic's husband. The Prosecution says, in short, that the SRK controlled the stadium, but if it didn't, in the view of the Trial Chamber, it makes no difference having regard to the undisputed area to the southeast of the stadium itself, immediately to the southeast, higher ground, including the police academy which was controlled by the SRK. No dispute about that. Your Honour, I should point out, excuse me -- I'm sorry, I should correct myself, General Karavelic said that it was the SRK that held the stadium together with local residents who also said that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: On the water collection incident, you said that the house at the mouth of the trench towards the tunnel, that the house was only 120 metres away of the spot of the incident. Is it possible that the that was an error and that it was directed towards the house and not towards the people queueing for the water?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, there is an issue of timing, that is when the tunnel opened, but first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I know that the tunnel at that time was not --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. I would hand over to Mr. Stamp to respond further to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, the brief answer, if it pleases you, Your Honour, is that the house could not have been the target because the house had no significance at the time of the shelling, so the issue of error in trying to target the house would not arise. But if there was another target, the question of error in so far as it may arise is in the realm of what is merely possible. One has to resort to the evidence and look at the evidence quite clearly of those persons who were there, who could speak of what is happening within the vicinity of the water line. There was no military target in the neighbourhood. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: The house was not a military target?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The house was not a military target at the time of the shelling. The house became a military target weeks after the shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: How many weeks?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: According to the witness Hadzic, construction of the trench from the houses started about ten days, I think he said, after the 31st of July, when the tunnel opened. That would put it at least three weeks after the incident. There is also a document presented by the Defence witness Rado Radinovic from the command of the ABiH, giving them instructions in taking steps for crossing the runway of the airport, and this document is dated sometime after the 12th of July, 1993. That also is proof indicating that the house and the tunnel were not in use and it confirms what the witness Hadzic said. The witness Karavelic also said the same thing that the tunnel, the house and the tunnel did not come in use until August. This is what Karavelic said, and Grebic another witness, Husein Grebic who was a part of the ABiH, he also confirmed that the tunnel was not in operation at that time. The important thing it is submitted is to look at the evidence as a sequence of events. The shelling occurred on the 12th of July. The tunnel opened on the 31st of July according to Hadzic or the 1st of August according to Karavelic. Because of the opening of the tunnel, people started to gather in various places in the area, and that is when it was determined that they would build a trench to the tunnel. The entry to the tunnel was some 300 metres from the incident. So I will concede that in respect to every single shooting with a firearm, even with a sniper rifle and shelling, there is always a possibility of error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Always. One has to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: That was not the question. The question was whether the SRK could be firing at the house because there was a construction, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Construction, it's submitted, did not begin until ten days after the opening of the tunnel and that construction or modification of the house, construction of a trench that led to the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes, of the trench. The house was at the mouth, let's say, of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Of the trench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Of the trench, okay. Thank you. We heard about the existence of a sniper rifles in general but yesterday, Mr. Ierace, speaking about one incident you said that the source of fire was just to the north of Ozrenska Street, do you remember that case in Ozrenska Street. And you said that the snipers were equipped with night sights. I couldn't find the source of that assertion about night sights.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I have a few minutes, I think I can find that specific reference. Perhaps I could indicate later on this morning what that page reference is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could the Defence respond to what the Prosecution has said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To a limited extent. We are putting questions to -- we are asking more or less for clarifications of what the parties have said but if there is an urgent need to respond, I'll give an opportunity, but done briefly. It's not a new debate we are in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I do it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Very simply, the Defence has always said that the chief question was the intent when it comes to shots. With regard to the first two incidents, I am not referring the second which was mentioned by Judge Nieto-Navia and one has to say that the truck in question had been requisitioned by the army. Secondly, Mr. Ierace said that it was hit because it was fired, and therefore, we shall have the cemeteries of cars painted red because everybody thought that -- the third question was the hospital. The killed soldier, he has according to -- it was to the Prosecution to show the presence of soldiers or not, and when such a building is fired at, one doesn't know where the shots are coming from. And my final point, and I shall leave the rest, et cetera, because it's not very important but I'm referring to the water line, the water line and the house. We are told that the trench was built later but the Defence wishes to say two things with this regard. When such a large tunnel is being built, it does not go unnoticed, and it is said that the Serbs had their intelligence sources and so they were perfectly aware of that. And when somebody digs something, there are usually teams and these teams are visible. That is, they are seen. It may be civilians who were forced to do that or somebody else, or soldiers, but they can be seen, and also it was said that five or seven hundred days of command. But how many water lines were there during all that time and how many water lines were fired -- were hit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... What I said before that a very short response was possible, that it became more or less a restart of the debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In response to the question asked by Judge Nieto-Navia, the page reference is 1934, the evidence of witness D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to give an opportunity to Judge El Mahdi to put questions to the parties. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] If I may, I'd like to ask the Prosecution to clarify a point in paragraph 62. Towards the very end of it. It is page 22, and I quote [In English] "The Prosecution submits that during the accused's command, the targeting of civilians through shelling and sniping was the principal instrument of this terrorisation and in this sense constituted a covert campaign. [No interpretation] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I didn't have a translation but I think my French is -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Could you explain to me what covert campaign means?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, it was sufficient on that occasion. Covert in the sense that the accused was not publicly proclaiming that he was targeting civilians. Campaign in the sense that at least in the English language, when one looks at the definition, I think it covers this pattern of behaviour. In other words, various resources were marshalled to achieve a particular objective. The behaviour of the accused was characterised by a degree of planning, allocation of his assets, the giving of orders to enable this end result, and that's what the Prosecution means by the use of the word "campaign." It wasn't an order given on one specific occasion. It involved the structure of his corps in order to achieve it. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you. And yet another question. You said, and I'm quoting you [In English] "May have been responsible for some isolated incident against their own civilians." [Interpretation] What do you mean exactly by some isolated? And elsewhere you said, not on a large scale. What do you mean by -- what do you think when you say not on a large scale? Does it mean dozens of incidents? Does it mean hundreds of incidents? Isolated? What do you mean by "isolated"? And what would be the legal consequences arising from your assertion that the Muslim party or the Bosnian Presidency at times fired at its own citizens?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. What I mean to convey by the use of the word "may" is an acceptance on the part of the Prosecution that there was evidence tendered before the Trial Chamber effectively -- well, to that effect. I have in mind, for example, evidence of suspicions entertained on the part of senior UN personnel, that there were occasions when there were instances, rather, when the -- some Bosnians, that is persons whom they suspected to be at least sympathisers with the Presidency cause who were responsible rather than elements on the SRK-held side of the confrontation lines. Another example, I think one I referred to this week, was the evidence of I think it was Commandant Hamill who said he looked at a tank round impact at Kosevo hospital in December 1993. And although it wasn't a full analysis that he did, his preliminary conclusion was that the round must have emanated from inside the city. It's important I think to always keep in mind that there has been no conclusive evidence in that regard, for instance, in relation to that incident, because there wasn't a full analysis. A number of scenarios, inconsistent with the conclusion that there was deliberate fire from within the confrontation lines have not been excluded, such as accident. The consequences? First, I think the next aspect to Your Honour's question was the extent of it. Can we quantify it? What does the Prosecution say as to quantification? The -- there was no doubt, the Prosecution submits, having regard to the evidence that if it happened, it constituted an absolute minority of the volume of fire that was directed at civilians either deliberately or indiscriminately, and I emphasise the use of the word "if", if it happened. The consequences at law, in terms of this trial, are these: One must keep in mind the specific charges against the accused, and the use that was made of the scheduled incidents, that is they were illustrative. Assuming that the Trial Chamber makes a finding of fact that civilians either may have been targeted from within the confrontation lines or were targeted from within the confrontation lines, and assuming that the Trial Chamber makes a further finding of fact contingent upon an earlier finding that it did happen, that the extent of it was absolutely minimal, it does not assist the accused at all in responding to the charges against him. As I indicated during the week, it's not a question of either-or. Rather as well as. Your Honour, in your question, you referred to the Presidency. In my submissions I was careful not to refer to the Presidency in making submissions on this topic because there is no link established between these incidents or the suggestion of these incidents and either the ABiH or other forces associated with the government itself. One recalls the, for instance, on a slightly different issue, the evidence of General Karavelic in relation to the suggestion that mobile mortars were fired -- were engaging in screen fire but firing to positions on SRK-held territory, and he said that he made every effort he could. He received such reports from the UN and made every effort he could to locate those units and was particularly frustrated by the suggestion that they were firing from the area of the state hospital because that was very close to his headquarters. But even so he was unable to arrive there on time. He and his forces. So again, if it happened, and certainly there is strong evidence that there was screen firing from the vicinity of the PTT and on occasions the Kosevo hospital, there is also strong evidence that there weren't units within the ABiH. So I think it's important that we keep that perspective. If it happened, there were persons within the confrontation lines, no strong evidence as to who they were associated with, ultimately it's of no assistance to the accused. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I'm proceeding along the same lines. Do you exclude whatever intervention of Croats? Because it seems that there were some indications that Croats changed camp during the events in 1992 to 1994. Would you exclude a possible intervention of the Croat side in the events around or within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. The -- while it's -- we understand that at various times during the armed conflict in Sarajevo, there were Bosnian Croatian units, the evidence is also that they were subsumed into the ABiH, that there was a Croatian unit set up. It seems that at some stages, there were independent units of Bosnian Croatian military operating but the evidence has never, during the trial, reached the point of establishing that such units were engaged relevantly, in terms of the targeting of civilians. Whatever military role they may have played when not a part of the ABiH seems to have been confined to legitimate military activities for the purposes of this trial, in other words there is no evidence that it went beyond that, in terms of the evidence we've heard in this trial. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you. And my last question has to do with the paramilitaries. It is quite possible that there are some indications in the record that for at least a certain period of time, they were uncontrollable and General Galic complained about their insubordination. Do you agree with that fact, that there were paramilitaries who acted independently of exact strict military structure and can you -- what can you say that as of such and such date, there are no more paramilitaries? Can you say that categorically and emphatically that as of such and such date there are no more paramilitaries who are outside who are not placed under the command of General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the second part of the question, I think it is possible to say that by the first few months, say by March, 1993, the evidence indicates that the accused did not have an insubordination problem with the -- within the SRK. To come to the first part of the question, while there is evidence that there were disciplinary issues from early September, when the accused assumed his command, there is absolutely no evidence at all that the insubordinate units were responsible for targeting civilians, contrary to the wishes of the accused. If I could put that another way, there is no suggestion in the evidence that the individuals or units with which the accused had a discipline problem were acting contrary to his orders in relation to the targeting of civilians. The witnesses called by the Defence who gave evidence of the insubordination, went on to qualify the issues involved, and the issues had nothing to do with that, with the targeting of civilians. The Defence has never called -- has not called a witness or pointed to a document or any other form of evidence which links the insubordinate units to that practice. The most prominent unit that might qualify for the term paramilitary in the SRK was Aleksic's unit, at the -- positioned at the Jewish cemetery, and of course, Colonel Indic described them as Chetniks. But again, typical of this aspect of the evidence in the trial, there was no suggestion that they were acting against the orders of the accused on the issue of civilians. Thank you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, very briefly. The Defence has the following comments. I note that the question was. Asked about legal consequences. We do not have the answer. That is not the proper answer. As for whether there is any evidence about active paramilitary units, I say yes, there is Kraljevic if not there, then on the other side. And where were those units -- whether those units or whether Croat units were responsible for the crisis at question, I would say that it is the Prosecutor who needs to prove that a particular fact is the fact that that was done. It's not up to the Defence to prove the contrary, that the accused had nothing to do with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a few more questions as well. First a question for the Prosecution. In the indictment, the unlawful attacks committed through sniping is speaking of deliberate attacks. At the same time, we find in some sniping incidents qualifications, as indiscriminate attacks. Would you -- is my understanding right that your explanation you gave in response to a question of one of my fellow judges on the incident where the butcher's truck was hit, would that be the explanation of how deliberate attacks relate to indiscriminate attacks?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think I used my words well earlier on. The Prosecution says that whether the -- whether civilians are targeted specifically, I think that's a better word, or indiscriminately, both types are deliberate. In the case of incident 13, the Prosecution does not know whether the shooter aimed at specifically the 15 year old or the father or both, but makes the observation that the evidence suggests that that was an instance of specific targeting, that one or both of them were specifically targeted. An example of indiscriminate fire is perhaps incident 10, where the target is the glowing window from Ozrenska Street. The shooter then presumably wasn't to know if there was even someone behind the light but fired indiscriminately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would still be a deliberate attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is a form of deliberateness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my next question would be the PTT building. The PTT building was not used by civilians. It served as the UN headquarters, as a matter of fact. Is it your view that when the PTT building was attacked, that that had any relevance in view of the counts of the indictment? Or is it just separate?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is some evidence that there were civilians operating in the PTT. If I could refer to two categories of such civilians, UN staff had civilians working for them. An example is the Bosnian Serbian secretary of General Abdel-Razek. We've heard other evidence as well of local staff. The second category are civilians who took shelter in the PTT billing, such as the mother of Milada Halili. That aside, if I could address, I think your fundamental point, you are correct in, as I discern your assumption, that that is not squarely related to the charges against the accused. Those charges are directed specifically at the civilian population of Sarajevo rather than the UN personnel who were nevertheless an unlawful target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's not the -- these are not the civilians you -- that was not part of the terror, that was not part of the counts of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you excuse me just for a moment, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. President. I think that's an important point. The Prosecution does not say that the objective of the campaign was to terrorise the UN personnel but rather the body of civilians who resided in Sarajevo separate from the UN personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one question? You said that the mother of one of the witnesses took shelter in the PTT building. It's my recollection that it was the post office, but was that same? Or she worked in the post office, as I remember, or am I totally wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the reference in the evidence was on occasion to the post office but specifically in relation to the PTT as well, but we didn't hear any other evidence to that same effect, so there is a -- it is a grey factual issue of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not of major importance I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No. I think the aspect of that which is most interesting is that she removed herself from the front line area because of personal safety considerations and placed herself more centrally in the city, in an institution that she thought would be safe and it didn't work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then another question for you, Mr. Ierace. What is exactly the position of the Prosecution in respect of the possibility of mortar units firing at their own initiative? Does the Prosecution accept that it would be reasonably possible that such firing at its own initiative took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There are some examples that come to mind from the evidence, such as Witness D with the drunken mortar units at Grbavica but I think there is another body of evidence that is more instructive and that is the evidence of the observations of UN personnel such as Henneberry, that he watched mortar units firing indiscriminately from Lima positions, I think Lima 7 was one that he nominated. You may recall, Mr. President, evidence that the crew would kick the mortar and then fire it. The Prosecution case in relation to that is that that was within the expected boundaries of behaviour entertained by the accused. A corps commander does not nominate mortar targets or artillery targets. A corps commander drafts a plan with the assistance of his operational staff. That plan then becomes the framework for his subordinates to operate under. The Prosecution case is that this behaviour by mortar units firing of their own initiative came within that plan. Other witnesses who observed such behaviour by mortar crews gave evidence on occasion that liaison staff from the headquarters were with them at the time that they made such observations. That is evidence which builds this -- is a foundation for the Prosecution's submission that the behaviour clearly would have been reported back to the headquarters through those officers who had brought the journalists and the like to those positions where they made those observations, and if it was contrary to the accused's wishes, then it would have stopped, and it didn't. So the accused on the evidence contemplated that crews would act in this fashion, of their own volition, from time to time, and that was acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you take it that those incidents would be reported, would you think that for those -- for this firing at own initiative, that it would be more appropriately to put that under responsibility under 7(1) or 7(3)?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have two more questions, one for the Defence and one for the Prosecution. I'd like to keep them for after the break so that the Prosecution also has an opportunity to inquire on the issue that we discussed before. Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Will we be allowed to respond to several issues in a minute very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As you did it before we could do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do it now, gladly, Mr. President. I've made a note of certain matters here and very briefly I'll return to the issue of the UN building. It seems that for the Prosecution this is part of the infliction of terror, the Defence takes note of that and that is all. Secondly, I'll quote what Mr. Ierace said, he said that the shots from the other side represented an absolute minority. My question is, first of all, how can one know about this, so no investigations were carried out, and how can one affirm this? Because no investigations were conducted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have to check but is it correct that terror was -- that the PTT building was given the place as just -- I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a minute ago, Mr. Ierace said that it was a matter of terrorising the civilian personnel who was working there and he mentioned the secretary of General Abdel-Razek so it means that these shots -- [no interpretation] [Microphone not activated] [English] was that the secretary of Mr. Abdel-Razek was within the building and that therefore there would be terror on that basis, at least that is what I heard myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not exactly what he said. Of course he mentioned the secretary of General Abdel-Razek but he did not -- he said at the end of his line, those charges are directly specifically at the civilian population of Sarajevo rather than to the UN personnel who were nevertheless an unlawful target. That's what he said. But the first mentioning of civilians in the building was, as far as I understood, a response to my question, and my question was that -- not being used by civilians, and I think it was a correction to my suggestion that there were no civilians in that building at all. But there is no suggestion that the attack on civilians within the PTT building was part of the terror. We will adjourn until 25 minutes to -- no, let's take half an hour. We will adjourn until 20 minutes to 1.00, and I assume that we will then finish in approximately not more than 20, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was about to ask two more questions to the parties. The first question would be for the Defence. What is the view of the Defence on the duties of the BiH authorities in view of evacuating civilians from where they lived if it was close to the confrontation lines and apart from what their duties, also, what is the legal basis for such duties?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. A very delicate question. And I think I see where you want to go with it. I think that the first basis is natural law. The right of people to be protected by their governments and by their states. I think that is the first basis. And now to answer the question as to whether it's Protocol I or Protocol II, what I can say is that it is certainly not Protocol I that is concerned, Protocol I upon which one should base oneself. We should base oneself on a very natural fact and that is the fact that it is not acceptable, if it is possible, to evacuate people, not to do so. That is the Defence's position, and I have to say with regard to this subject, Mr. President, that if, for example, there are military means, equipment, such as lorries and one allows civilians to enter, one is taking risks, and this is by no means Protocol I that is concerned. We should see which -- what is really pertinent is probably Protocol II but the Defence will not express or is not expressing a definite position with regard to this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I know what is not a legal basis and you say the natural law is as a matter of fact the basis on which the duty rests. Is that -- no further sources? No further authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps there are but I don't think it is for the Defence to formulate them. It is obvious that it's a principle. It is obvious that within the framework of Protocol II, this principle is likewise set forth and there is a decision here and contains an argument which is founded on an ad absurdum argument and we are shown that even in the case of Protocol II we don't see why a state in the case of an internal conflict, would protect its civilians to a lesser extent than in the case of an international conflict. We are all well aware of this fact but we are saying that it is not Protocol I that is applicable and we remain open to other possibilities. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... apply but on the other hand, there is not -- it's not well understandable why civilians should be less protected in an internal conflict as they would be in an international conflict. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It could be summarised like this, to the extent that if we interpret both protocols in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecution, Mr. Ierace, you just have explained to us what you understood the campaign to be, you talked about a degree of planning, allocation of assets, giving of orders to enable the result envisaged. What I'd like to ask you is, in the opinion of the Prosecution, is it possible that the accused could be held responsible under Article 7(3) in his position as commander, for a campaign which would then be or have to have been orchestrated or organised by his subordinates, that means a campaign -- let me just -- under Article 7(3), I think it's fair to say that it's the subordinates who commit the acts necessary to qualify as a crime, and under Article 7(3) it's the commander who did not prevent them to do so or did not punish them if they had done so, so I'm asking you how you see the situation where a military commander would be held responsible for a campaign of shelling and sniping under Article 7(3).

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in that situation, it doesn't matter what the motivation was for these subordinates to engage in those unlawful activities. It doesn't matter whether the motivation was, as it happens, a campaign organised by the accused's senior subordinates. What matters is that they engaged in unlawful conduct, they were secondly subordinate to the accused, and thirdly, the accused failed to exercise his responsibilities under 7(3). Mr. President, I think it's appropriate also to observe that in certain circumstances, 7(3) can be transformed into 7(1) and this is such a circumstance, in particular the duration of the behaviour, the unlawful behaviour, by the subordinates. Put simply, if the accused becomes aware that his subordinates are engaged in unlawful activity and declines to take steps available to him to not only punish them but also prevent them from continuing to engage in such activity, then one can conclude that effectively that 7(3) behaviour is transformed into 7(1), he knows about it, he chooses to allow it to continue, when that happens for such an extended period of time, the distinction between 7(1) and 7(3) blurs to a point where it effectively becomes 7(1). Specifically, one can then conclude that that behaviour has been adopted by him and that brings it within 7(1).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that still would be a situation where the and I'll repeat your words, where the degree of planning and allocation of assets and giving of orders would be on the subordinate level but finally by accepting that this happens at a lower level, that it would fall into 7(3) and if that takes too long, then finally, you say that could convert more or less in 7(1).

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, he adopts it by knowingly failing to act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. These were my questions. I gave an opportunity to the Prosecution to reflect for half an hour more on the issues regarding the 22nd of May, 1992 agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before Mr. Mundis responds to that opportunity, might I add in relation to the last issue that the transformation of 7(3) behaviour into 7(1) behaviour was something referred to in our pre-trial brief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, with respect to the 22 May, 1992 agreement, the Prosecution has three brief remarks, final remarks, to make. First, the Prosecution would note that in the Blaskic judgement of 3 March, 2000, rendered by Trial Chamber I, in the context of an internal armed conflict between -- or involving Croatian, Bosnian Croat forces, the Trial Chamber in that case accepted the 22 May, 1992 agreement as being the basis upon which, or one of the two bases upon which Articles 51 and 52 of Additional Protocol I were applied with respect to that conflict. Certainly that would be one factor that the Prosecution would ask this Trial Chamber to take into consideration. You will find references to that agreement in the Blaskic judgement at paragraphs 80, 81, 172, and 173. With respect to the issue of ratification, Ian Brownlie in his treatis entitled the Principles of Public International Law, addresses the issue of ratification and specifically states that ratification involves two procedural acts. The first one he describes as being a constitutional act, that is an act of the appropriate organ of the state, and the second act being an international procedure which he characterises as bringing a treaty into force by a formal exchange or deposit of the instruments of ratification. He goes on to state that this is an important act involving consent to be bound. He goes on, however, and I will quote, "Everything depends on the intention of the parties where this is ascertainable." He concludes by citing of course to Article 14 of the Vienna Convention whereby there is reference to ratification being ascertained from the intention of the parties to the agreement, and that's at page 607 in Principles of Public International Law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I couldn't heard the name of the author.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ian Brownlie. The third point which the Prosecution would point to is that in the event the Trial Chamber and we have briefed this issue but I think it merits brief recitation. In the event the Trial Chamber determines that the agreement is not in effect, of course the interlocutory appeals decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Strugar case which this Trial Chamber, I think, is aware of clearly indicates that Articles 50 and 51 of Additional Protocol I reflect customary international law and that Article 13 of Additional Protocol II reflects customary international law and so we would rely on that as a fall-back position in the event that the Trial Chamber finds the agreement not to be applicable. One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, as a final point, I note in the Defence pre-trial brief, the heading at page 43, status of additional or excuse me, status of Article 51 of Additional Protocol I and Article 13 of Additional Protocol II as laws or customs of war, paragraphs 8.10 and 8.11, and in particular, paragraph 8.11 of the Defence pre-trial brief, where the following sentence occurs: "The Defence is not disputing the fact that both parties to the armed conflict were bound to uphold provisions of the Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocols I and II."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis that's what I referred to as a matter of fact when I said that the parties did agree on the applicability and do not agree any more. That's -- thank you for your explanation. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Mr. President, I wanted to say in fact that we raised this matter, this problem, but what I would like to underline very briefly if you will allow me to do so, is that I'll leave here far more wiser than before but it's not a matter of ratification here. It's a matter of something else. It's a matter of transmitting, of formal acceptance, as well as it has been in the declaration in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then all the questions of the bench have been answered and we have come to the moment where this trial is concluded and where the Chamber will have to prepare its judgement. We spent well over 200 days in this courtroom, mostly in this courtroom. We spent these 200 days with many people. Everyone having his own task in this trial. Not only the Prosecution and the Defence team, but also the interpreters. Without them the trial would be totally impossible. The same is true for the technical assistance we have from those who are in the technical booth. But the same is true as well for security, for the representative of the registry, who has been with us for all these days. Those supporting the chambers, the legal officers, the ushers who have assisted us during all these times, and the transcribers who have put on paper whatever was said in this courtroom. There is one person in this courtroom I have not mentioned yet and that's you, General Galic. We have not often heard your voice. To some extent that is a consequence of the procedural system that has been adopted in this Tribunal. To some extent it is also a consequence of the decisions the Defence has taken, decisions of course that are fully respected by this Chamber, but it resulted in not having heard your voice very often. At the same time, of course, we the Chamber is aware of how important these days have been for you, because you were here, you were charged by the Prosecution, you were defended by Defence team. So therefore although we might not have heard your voice very often, that does not mean that you were not in the centre of our attention all these more than 200 days. I'd like to thank all those who have participated in this trial. The Chamber has very much appreciated the seriousness with which everyone has fulfilled its task in this trial, the way you performed your duties, of course duties that are not the same, duties that are quite different Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. We have had good days and sometimes we had days that were a little bit less good but nevertheless, the Chamber is highly appreciative of the way that everyone contributed to this trial. The Chamber will have to deliver judgement. The Chamber will try to do that as soon as it can, in order not to -- in order to prevent that the long waiting will be an extra burden, first of all for, of course for you, General Galic, but also for the parties. On the other hand, I cannot give you a clear indication on when we will deliver judgement.
